summary: 3 stories. Added Treasury’s fiscal 2026 deficit report. The technology selloff and Hormuz-related oil risks remain in their existing stories. stories.headline: US markets are weighed down by an extended sell-off in the tech sector
stories.dek: A week of losses in technology shares brought attention to AI investment funding and inflation-sensitive borrowing costs.
tldr: U.S. technology shares extended a selloff on Friday, leaving major indexes with one of their weakest weeks in recent months.
The Associated Press and Reuters linked pressure on technology names to questions about AI investment, data-center borrowing and interest-rate risks.
The market move does not establish that AI demand has fallen or that planned infrastructure investment has been cancelled.

body.text: U.S. technology shares continued falling through Friday, and major indexes recorded one of their weakest weekly performances since late June, according to the Associated Press. Its report cited concerns about the durability of the AI investment boom as one pressure on chipmakers and other technology stocks.

Reuters also reported declines in AI-linked shares and investor attention to the debt used by data-center operators to expand computing capacity. CoreWeave was among the borrowers facing closer scrutiny.

The selling came as investors weighed financing costs alongside inflation and the outlook for interest rates. Falling share prices alone do not show that demand for AI has weakened or that data-center projects have been cancelled.

Further evidence will come from companies’ financing plans, capital spending and results. Current coverage describes market performance and investor concerns, while the direction of future earnings and infrastructure investment remains open.

stories.whyItMatters: The selloff brings financing costs and the expected returns on AI infrastructure into focus. Market prices reflect current investor concerns, but do not establish that AI demand or planned capital spending has turned down.
stories.editorNote: Reports market movements and stated concerns without treating them as proof of lower demand or cancelled projects.

stories.headline: Brent oil touches $110 as Iran escalates Hormuz attacks, Ukraine vows to hit Russian refineries
stories.dek: Oil markets faced competing supply risks from the Gulf and Russia as conflict-related shipping reports remained incomplete.
tldr: CNBC reported that Brent crude touched $110 a barrel amid rising risks around the Strait of Hormuz and renewed threats to Russian refinery sites.
BBC and AP reported increasing attack notices near the strait but also said underreporting makes the scale difficult to determine.
The available coverage does not establish how much oil transport was disrupted or whether the price move will persist.

body.text: Brent crude touched $110 a barrel, CNBC reported, as it cited escalating attacks near the Strait of Hormuz and Ukraine’s stated intention to target Russian refineries. The report linked both developments to concerns about supply routes.

BBC Verify reported a rise in ships reporting attacks near Hormuz and a slowdown in oil exports. The Associated Press said the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency could not reliably count all incidents because some vessels do not report suspected attacks.

These reports describe a security backdrop that can heighten uncertainty around transport, but incident reports are incomplete and do not by themselves measure lost oil volumes. The available coverage does not provide a full accounting of actual shipment delays or supply shortfalls.

The key unresolved questions are whether passage and exports remain constrained and how much other supply routes can compensate. This coverage reports current prices and security concerns; it does not establish a future price direction.

stories.whyItMatters: Risks near Hormuz are relevant to oil markets, but incomplete attack reporting makes the scale of any physical disruption uncertain. Current price moves do not establish what supply or prices will do next.
stories.editorNote: Labels the reports as context for current pricing and does not imply a forecast or quantified supply loss.

stories.headline: U.S. budget deficit swells to almost $2 trillion for fiscal 2026, up 12% in a single year
stories.dek: Treasury figures showed a $1.992 trillion deficit for the fiscal year ended September 30, compared with $1.775 trillion in fiscal 2025.
tldr: The U.S. budget deficit reached $1.992 trillion in fiscal 2026, up $217 billion, or about 12%, from fiscal 2025.
CNBC and Reuters reported that Treasury Department figures showed the shortfall was the largest in five years.
Tariff refunds and debt-service costs were among the reported factors, but the annual total does not establish a future deficit path.

body.text: The United States ended fiscal 2026, which closed on September 30, with a $1.992 trillion budget deficit, according to Treasury figures reported by CNBC and Reuters. The shortfall was $217 billion higher than the $1.775 trillion deficit in fiscal 2025.

The reports said the increase was about 12% and described the result as the largest deficit in five years. Reuters cited tariff refunds and record debt-service spending among factors behind the annual change.

The deficit is the difference between federal outlays and receipts over the fiscal year. It measures annual borrowing need, but one year’s result does not establish how the balance will change in subsequent fiscal years.

The contribution of individual policy changes and the outlook for interest costs and receipts remain subjects for further analysis. The Treasury’s next monthly statement will provide the first data for fiscal 2027, but this release alone does not establish a projection.

stories.whyItMatters: The larger annual shortfall adds to attention on federal borrowing and debt-service costs. Its longer-term implications depend on future receipts, spending and interest expenses rather than this total alone.
stories.editorNote: Uses Treasury figures as reported by CNBC and Reuters; does not infer a future deficit trajectory from the annual result.
